values: Start here: your first-day guide to launching YOW
You do not need to know how to code. Your job is to make decisions, follow safe test instructions, and report exactly what you see.
What you do each evening

1. Use the reserved 8:30–9:30 PM block.
2. Open the Daily Guide tab and find today's date.
3. Read only that row.
4. Copy its full Codex prompt into Codex.
5. Follow one instruction at a time.
6. Record Done, In progress, or Blocked.
7. Stop for the day. If you miss an evening, move that task to the next available evening instead of doubling up.
What Codex does for you

Codex reads and edits code, runs terminal commands, prepares safe test data, explains unfamiliar screens, records evidence, updates the roadmap, and tells you whether a task really passed. You should not be expected to diagnose code, database, deployment, or payment problems yourself.
Your four safety rules

1. Never paste passwords, API keys, recovery codes, or secret values into chat or the workbook.
2. Never test deletion or billing with your owner/admin account. Use the named test account.
3. If the screen does not match the instruction, stop and tell Codex what you see. Do not guess.
4. Never enable real paid checkout before the final launch-day instruction.
What the Status choices mean

Not started: you have not begun.
In progress: you started, but a safe next step remains.
Blocked: you cannot continue safely; write the exact reason in Notes.
Done: Codex confirmed the required result, evidence was saved, and the roadmap was updated when needed.
If you finish early or a task does not pass

Finish early: record the evidence, mark the row Done, add the real completion date to Notes, then continue with the next row that is not Done. Keep the original order even when working ahead.

Cannot pass safely: mark the row Blocked, copy the error or screenshot into Codex, and stop. A failed hard gate moves launch by one week. It does not remove the check, shorten the marketing runway, or justify risking customer data.
Beta removal in plain English

16 November: stop giving Beta access to new people and remove Beta as a public plan. Existing testers keep their access and exports.
16–27 November: market the upcoming launch while checkout stays off.
30 November: after the final checks, enable checkout and place existing Beta testers into the approved 30-day notice path. Never mass-delete or abruptly revoke their data.
How to import the calendar file

Apple Calendar: File → Import → choose YOW-Launch-Calendar-Beginner.ics → place it in a new calendar named YOW Launch.
Google Calendar: Settings → Import & export → Import → choose the .ics file → select or create a YOW Launch calendar.
Outlook: Add calendar → Upload from file → choose the .ics file.
Every entry reserves 8:30–9:30 PM Europe/London time. Weekend entries are lighter preparation, review, or catch-up blocks.

Plain-English glossary
You do not need to memorise these terms. Use this page when a word in the plan is unfamiliar.
Term
What it means
Why you care
App / application
The YOW software people use in a browser or as a downloaded desktop program.
This is the product you are preparing to sell.
Build
A packaged version of the current code that can be opened and tested.
A successful build means the code can be turned into a usable app; it does not prove every feature works.
QA
Quality assurance: deliberately testing the product and recording what passed or failed.
QA is how you avoid discovering serious problems after customers pay.
Automated test
A small program that checks expected behaviour automatically.
It catches repeat problems quickly, but it cannot replace every real-person test.
Smoke test
A short check of the most important path, such as sign in, write, save, and export.
If this fails, deeper testing should stop until the basic path is repaired.
Production
The live YOW website and live customer data.
Actions here can affect real people, so the plan tells you when to stop and ask.
Preview / staging
A non-public or test copy used before changing production.
It lets you rehearse safely.
Deploy
Publish a tested version of the app or backend so the live service uses it.
Code changes are not live until deployed.
Database
The organised storage holding accounts, projects, and other cloud information.
Unsafe database changes can lose or expose customer work.
Supabase
The service YOW uses for sign-in, cloud database, storage, and backend functions.
Several owner-only launch checks happen in its dashboard.
Migration
A versioned instruction that changes the database structure or security rules.
It must be applied and verified before matching app code depends on it.
RLS
Row Level Security: database rules controlling which signed-in user may read or change each row.
Correct RLS prevents one customer seeing another customer's data.
Stripe
The payment service used for checkout, subscriptions, refunds, and billing events.
It must grant access only after verified payment.
Webhook
A secure message sent automatically from Stripe to YOW when a payment event happens.
YOW uses it to grant, renew, cancel, or revoke paid access.
Environment variable / secret
A private configuration value stored outside the code, such as an API key.
Never paste these values into chat, screenshots, or the workbook.
API
A controlled way for one piece of software to request work or data from another.
YOW's browser, backend, Supabase, Stripe, and AI providers communicate through APIs.
Release candidate
The exact version proposed for launch after feature work stops.
Only blocker fixes should change it before launch.
Rollback
Return production to the last known-good version after a serious launch problem.
It is the safe exit if launch behaviour differs from rehearsal.
Backup
A separate copy that can restore data after damage or deletion.
Take one before risky tests or launch changes.
Clean-machine test
Install and use the app on a computer that has not been prepared by the developer.
It reveals missing files, permissions, or instructions that a development computer hides.
Hash / checksum
A long fingerprint calculated from a file.
Matching hashes prove the downloaded installer is the exact approved file.
Entitlement
The server-controlled record of what a plan allows, such as desktop access or AI tools.
A user must never be able to grant paid access to themselves.
Beta
Pre-launch access used for testing with real users before normal paid launch.
Closing Beta enrollment is different from deleting or abruptly revoking existing testers.
Hard gate
A check that must pass before the planned launch can continue.
A failed hard gate moves the date; it is not skipped.
CSP
Content Security Policy: browser rules limiting where scripts, images, and connections may come from.
It reduces the damage malicious or accidental third-party content can cause.
